alalal-e91513-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 2: whether it ever sufficed to believe of God that he exists and rewards those who seek him.

alalal-e91513-d1e115.summary: States the second question: whether believing that God exists and rewards those who seek him ever sufficed.

alalal-e91513-d1e124.summary: Introduces arguments that it did suffice.

alalal-e91513-d1e130.summary: First argument: the Apostle says so (Hebrews 11:6).

alalal-e91513-d1e135.summary: Second argument: these suffice for tending to God through knowledge of first truth: believing that he is shows where one tends, believing that he rewards moves by hope and love of reward.

alalal-e91513-d1e151.summary: Third argument: appetitive motion needs only apprehension of the delightful and appetite for it; believing that God is gives the first, believing he rewards the second.

alalal-e91513-d1e173.summary: Fourth argument: in innocence Adam did not foresee his fall, and without the fall no mediator was needed, so he had to believe nothing about the mediator; the same applies to other articles.

alalal-e91513-d1e195.summary: Fifth argument: after the fall there was no open prophecy or known revelation, and articles exceed reason, so reason was not bound to them; believing what nature dictated sufficed.

alalal-e91513-d1e217.summary: Sixth argument: suppose someone without revelation, under natural law or Moses' law, does what natural law dictates; he will be saved, as Romans 2:27 says the uncircumcised who fulfil the law will judge the transgressor.

alalal-e91513-d1e240.summary: Since natural reason says nothing about the mediator, one need believe only the two things reason dictates.

alalal-e91513-d1e249.summary: Sed contra: Lombard's text proves by many authorities that faith in the mediator was necessary.

alalal-e91513-d1e260.summary: Second sed contra: to be healed one must know the disease and its nature, and Anselm proves it was such that only one who is God and man could satisfy for it; so the liberator and mediator had to be believed.

alalal-e91513-d1e278.summary: Third sed contra: all who were saved from the beginning knew they were saved by God's grace, not their merits, and all grace comes through Jesus Christ (John 1:17), so they had to believe that a saviour would come and satisfy for man.

alalal-e91513-d1e298.summary: Solution: since the fall, no one was ever saved by grace except through faith in the mediator. The mediator can be considered in particular, in the sacraments by which he mediated, or universally, as mediating in whatever way he willed. Following Hugh, the ancients were not bound to believe explicitly in the first way, but all in the second; in the first way only those who received revelation and those they instructed. In innocence Adam had clearer knowledge than we of the divinity and the eternal distinction of persons, but not of reconciliation through Christ.
claims: Since the fall, salvation has always required faith in the mediator, at least in a general way.
Explicit faith in the particular mysteries of mediation was required only of those who received revelation or instruction.

alalal-e91513-d1e350.summary: Reply to the first: this suffices for approaching God, but 'that he is' does not mean his existence in general, which reason investigates, but as determined in certain articles by revelation; 'that he rewards' pertains to hope and love.
claims: 'That God is' in Hebrews 11:6 means God as specified by revealed articles, not a merely rational theism.

alalal-e91513-d1e375.summary: Reply to the second: 'that he is' in general does not suffice to show the end as faith tends to it; it must be specified in distinct articles, since general knowledge does not move, but distinct knowledge of a particular's properties does.
claims: Only specified knowledge of God, not general knowledge, moves toward him as end.

alalal-e91513-d1e397.summary: This also answers the next argument.

alalal-e91513-d1e404.summary: Reply to the fourth: what sufficed for Adam does not suffice for one who knows he is in sin and cannot cure himself; and Albert holds that even Adam in his first state believed certain articles, not only God's existence in general, though not those concerning the mediator.
claims: Adam in innocence believed certain articles but not those concerning the mediator.

alalal-e91513-d1e426.summary: Reply to the fifth: it supposes a falsehood, since Hugh says signs of healing through Christ's offering, and so revelation, began from the start of the world, as in Abel's sacrifice (Hebrews 11:4) and thereafter.
claims: Signs and revelation of the mediator existed from the beginning, starting with Abel's sacrifice.

alalal-e91513-d1e455.summary: Reply to the sixth: it is commonly said that no one who did what lay in him to prepare himself failed to receive revelation from God, teaching from inspired men, or a sign of the mediator; Albert agrees, because of God's providence, which provides goods to all equally and offers them to all who are ready to receive.
claims: God provides the necessary revelation or sign of the mediator to all who do what lies in them.

alalal-e91513.summary: Article 2 asks whether believing that God exists and rewards those who seek him (Hebrews 11:6) ever sufficed for salvation, given Adam's innocence, the lack of open revelation after the fall, and the case of someone who keeps the natural law. Albert holds that since the fall no one has been saved except through faith in the mediator. All were bound to believe in the mediator universally, but explicit faith in the particular mysteries was required only of those who received revelation or instruction. The 'that he is' of Hebrews means God as specified by revealed articles, not rational theism, since only specified knowledge moves one toward God. Adam believed some articles, though not those about the mediator. Signs of Christ's offering appeared from Abel onward. God's providence gives revelation or signs to all who do what lies in them.
claims: Since the fall, salvation has always required faith in the mediator, at least universally.
Explicit faith in the particular mysteries was required only of those who received revelation or instruction.
God provides the necessary revelation or sign to all who do what lies in them.
